cards.front: What should you know about blind spots?
cards.back: Blind spots are nearby areas that the interior and outside rear-view mirrors do not show.

cards.front: What should you know about lane-change search?
cards.back: Before changing lanes, check the mirrors and turn your head over the shoulder toward the intended lane to check blind spots.

cards.front: What should you know about lane-change gap and signal?
cards.back: Find a traffic gap, signal and look again toward the lane you intend to enter.

cards.front: What should you know about completing a lane change?
cards.back: Adjust speed and steering as you enter the new lane, then cancel the signal.

cards.front: What should you know about freeway merge search?
cards.back: On a freeway entrance, watch the vehicle ahead and use an over-shoulder check and outside mirrors to locate a merging gap.

cards.front: What should you know about freeway merge speed?
cards.back: Signal and accelerate in the entrance lane to the speed of freeway traffic before merging, then cancel the signal.

cards.front: What should you know about exit preparation?
cards.back: Know the intended exit and move toward its lane early enough to avoid a sudden lane change.

cards.front: What should you know about using an exit lane?
cards.back: Maintain speed on the main roadway, signal into the deceleration lane, and slow there while observing its posted speed.

cards.front: What should you know about missed exit?
cards.back: If you miss an exit, continue to the next one instead of using a median opening reserved for emergency and public-safety vehicles.

cards.front: What should you know about passing search?
cards.back: Before passing, check for approaching vehicles and use mirrors and an over-shoulder look to check vehicles following or already passing.

cards.front: What should you know about entering the passing lane?
cards.back: When a pass is safe, signal and move smoothly into the passing lane while adjusting speed as needed.

cards.front: What should you know about return after passing?
cards.back: Continue a pass until both headlights of the passed vehicle appear in the rear-view mirror, then signal and return smoothly while maintaining an appropriate speed.

cards.front: What should you know about being passed?
cards.back: When another driver passes, hold your lane and keep a steady speed so the pass can be completed.

cards.front: What should you know about oncoming traffic and passing?
cards.back: Do not start a pass when a vehicle is approaching from the opposite direction.

cards.front: What should you know about limited passing view?
cards.back: Do not pass when a curve or hill blocks the view ahead.

cards.front: What should you know about passing at intersections?
cards.back: Do not attempt to pass at an intersection.

cards.front: What should you know about passing before crossings or bridges?
cards.back: Do not attempt a pass before a railroad crossing or bridge.

cards.front: What should you know about passing lane on multilane roads?
cards.back: On a multilane two-way road, the far-left lane is intended for passing slower vehicles when the pass will not interfere with traffic in either direction.

cards.front: What should you know about shoulder passing?
cards.back: Never use a roadway shoulder to pass, whether the shoulder is paved or unpaved.

cards.front: What should you know about double-yellow passing rule?
cards.back: On a two-lane two-way road with double solid yellow centerlines, passing is prohibited except for a safe pass of a slow-moving vehicle such as a bicycle or a vehicle with a slow-moving-vehicle sign.

cards.front: What should you know about double-yellow driveway turn?
cards.back: A driver may cross double solid yellow centerlines to turn left into a driveway when it is safe.

cards.front: What should you know about solid-and-dashed passing side?
cards.back: On a two-lane two-way road with a solid-and-dashed yellow centerline, passing is allowed only from the dashed-line side and is prohibited from the solid-line side.

cards.front: What should you know about center turn lane restrictions?
cards.back: A shared center left-turn lane serves left turns from either direction and must not be used for passing, merging into traffic or through travel.

cards.front: What should you know about railroad warning signs?
cards.back: Railroad crossings may be identified by a round yellow sign bearing a cross and the letters R R, or by a white crossbuck labeled Railroad Crossing.

cards.front: What should you know about railroad active warnings?
cards.back: Some railroad crossings have train-activated flashing red lights and may also have a gate.

cards.front: What should you know about railroad warning response?
cards.back: At a railroad warning sign, slow down and prepare to stop if you see or hear an approaching train.

cards.front: What should you know about train stopping distance?
cards.back: For an approaching train, stop between fifteen and fifty feet from the crossing.

cards.front: What should you know about waiting after a train?
cards.back: Wait for the train to pass and for warning signals to stop before crossing the rails.

cards.front: What should you know about crossbuck-only approach?
cards.back: Where only pavement markings or crossbucks mark a crossing, approach slowly and be ready to stop for a train seen or heard.

cards.front: What should you know about railroad track obstruction?
cards.back: Do not stop a vehicle on railroad tracks or try to cross ahead of an approaching train.

cards.front: What should you know about railroad stop sign?
cards.back: Every vehicle must stop before proceeding through a railroad crossing marked by a stop sign.

cards.front: What should you know about school-bus amber lights?
cards.back: Four flashing amber bus lights, two at each end, warn that the bus is preparing to stop; drivers need not stop for amber alone but should prepare for the bus to stop.

cards.front: What should you know about school-bus red lights?
cards.back: When a school bus stops to load or unload children, its amber lights change to four flashing red lights, with two at each end.

cards.front: What should you know about school-bus stop arm?
cards.back: A school bus may extend a flashing stop arm from its left side, but the absence of that arm does not remove the stopping requirement.

cards.front: What should you know about school bus on fewer than four lanes?
cards.back: On a road with fewer than four lanes, traffic approaching a stopped school bus from either direction must stop at least ten feet from it until the bus moves or its driver signals permission to proceed.

cards.front: What should you know about school bus on four or more lanes?
cards.back: On a road with at least four lanes, only traffic going the bus's direction must stop behind a stopped school bus and wait until the bus moves.

cards.front: What should you know about reporting illegal bus passing?
cards.back: A bus driver who believes a vehicle passed unlawfully may report its plate and location to law enforcement for driver identification.

cards.front: What should you know about designated parking?
cards.back: Use a designated parking area and face the direction of traffic on your side of the street.

cards.front: What should you know about right-curb parking distance?
cards.back: Park parallel within twelve inches of the right curb.

cards.front: What should you know about one-way curb parking?
cards.back: On a one-way street, parallel parking is allowed within twelve inches of either curb.

cards.front: What should you know about angled parking?
cards.back: Painted lines mark spaces intended for angled parking.

cards.front: What should you know about parking restriction markers?
cards.back: Check signs and painted curbs for parking prohibitions or limits.

cards.front: What should you know about accessible parking authorization?
cards.back: Do not use a wheelchair-marked accessible parking space without an issued removable windshield placard or accessible license plate.

cards.front: What should you know about sidewalk stopping restriction?
cards.back: Do not stop, park or stand a motor vehicle on a sidewalk unless needed to avoid a traffic conflict or to follow police or traffic-control directions.

cards.front: What should you know about driveway stopping restriction?
cards.back: Do not stop, park or stand in front of a public or private driveway unless avoiding a traffic conflict or following police or traffic-control directions requires it.

cards.front: What should you know about intersection and crosswalk parking clearance?
cards.back: Except when avoiding a traffic conflict or obeying police or traffic-control directions, do not stop, park or stand in an intersection or crosswalk or within twenty feet of either.

cards.front: What should you know about fire hydrant parking clearance?
cards.back: Do not stop, park or stand within ten feet of a fire hydrant unless needed to avoid a traffic conflict or to comply with police or traffic-control directions.

cards.front: What should you know about parked vehicle clearance?
cards.back: Keep at least one foot from another parked vehicle when stopping, parking or standing, except as needed to avoid traffic conflict or obey police or traffic-control directions.

cards.front: What should you know about double parking?
cards.back: Do not stop, park or stand beside a vehicle already stopped or parked along the street edge or curb, except for traffic-conflict avoidance or police or traffic-control directions.

cards.front: What should you know about signed no-stopping location?
cards.back: Do not stop, park or stand where a sign prohibits stopping unless avoiding a traffic conflict or obeying police or traffic-control directions requires it.

cards.front: What should you know about hill-parking sequence in the handbook?
cards.back: For hill parking, the handbook directs turning the front wheels toward the curb side, selecting park, setting the parking brake and switching off the engine.
